title: Contractive Diffusion Policies
one_liner: Make action diffusion resistant to learned-model errors by adding a penalty that keeps nearby noisy actions flowing toward similar clean actions.
lead: When a robot learns from past experience to pick actions, diffusion models work by gradually cleaning up noise-covered actions. But tiny errors in that cleaning process pile up, making the robot confused about which action to pick. This paper adds a penalty that pulls nearby noisy actions toward the same destination, like a funnel, so errors do not throw the action choice wildly off course.

problem.h2: The problem: noisy paths lead the robot astray
paras: Diffusion policies work by starting with a fully noisy action (random garbage) and gradually removing noise step by step until a clean action emerges. Each step uses a learned model to predict how much noise to strip away. This is like a very long, wobbly path through a fog.

In image generation, small stumbles along the path do not matter—a blurry spot in the corner goes unnoticed. But for robot actions, a tiny mistake compounds. If the denoising at step 50 is wrong, then step 51 starts from the wrong place, making step 52 even worse. By step 200, the robot is doing something completely different from what was intended.

A beginner might just use more training data to get the denoising model perfect. But that is expensive, and it does not solve the real problem: even a small error in the learned model is inevitable, and stacking 200 steps of small errors breaks the action choice.

callout.html: Contractive Diffusion Policies add a penalty during training that makes the denoising path less sensitive to mistakes, so small errors do not throw the final action off course.

panels.title: 1. How diffusion denoises an action
panels.caption: A diffusion path starts with pure noise and gradually removes it across 200 steps to reveal an action.

panels.title: 2. Error piles up: nearby starting points diverge
panels.caption: Two tiny-different starting noises follow the denoising path. Small mistakes at each step make them drift apart—the fork widens.

panels.title: 3. The solution: add a contraction penalty
panels.viz_args: Penalty pushes nearby paths to stay together
panels.caption: During training, penalize the learned denoising model if it would push similar starting points far apart.

panels.title: 4. Nearby paths now funnel together
panels.caption: With the contraction penalty, two nearby noisy starts now follow converging paths that merge—errors do not compound.

panels.title: 5. The robot picks a stable, reliable action
panels.caption: Because the denoising path forgives small mistakes, tiny errors stay tiny and do not wreck the final action.

steps.text: Train a model to predict how much noise to remove at each step, guided by offline data the robot collected.
For each batch of training data, calculate how the denoising prediction changes when you tweak the input slightly—this is the Jacobian.
If the Jacobian is too large, nearby inputs would diverge—add a penalty to the training loss to shrink it.
Combine the denoising error loss with the contraction penalty, weighted by a tuning knob, and optimize.
At test time, follow the denoising path step by step; the trained contraction keeps nearby flows funneled together, so small errors stay small.

object.h2: What the paper changes: the denoising sensitivity
paras: The paper modifies one specific part of the learned denoising model: how much the output changes when the input changes slightly. In normal diffusion, the model is trained only to predict noise removal accurately—it can be very sensitive to tiny input tweaks. Contractive Diffusion Policies adds a second objective: make the denoising output insensitive to small input changes. This is called making the function 'contractive.'

hidden.name: contraction magnitude
paras: Contraction measures how much the denoising model's output would change if you nudge the input slightly. Mathematically, it is the largest eigenvalue (the strongest 'stretch') of the Jacobian—the matrix that tells you how sensitive the output is to each input direction. A low contraction means nearby inputs stay close; a high contraction means they diverge. The paper estimates contraction by computing this largest eigenvalue during training.

Why measure it? Because contraction directly controls error sensitivity. If contraction is high, a small mistake at one denoising step gets amplified at the next step, and errors compound. If contraction is low, errors stay local and do not blow up over 200 steps.

heat.caption: Darker means higher contraction (more sensitive to input changes). Early and late steps need tighter control.

reads.html: Imagine two twin robots with identical sensors and memories, but one's sensor is zoomed in by 0.01 percent. After 200 denoising steps, how far apart are their chosen actions? If contraction is low, they still agree. If high, they choose opposite actions. Low contraction means tiny sensor differences do not widen into different final actions.

The paper uses the largest eigenvalue of the score-Jacobian matrix to quantify contraction. During training, it computes the Jacobian of the learned score function with respect to the noisy action at each denoising time step, then applies a loss term that penalizes eigenvalues larger than 1.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: funneling error into safety
paras: The core insight is that denoising is a dynamical system. At each step, the learned model takes in a noisy action and outputs a slightly cleaner one. If the model is contractive, then two paths that start close together will stay close—like two rivers flowing into a funnel. This means errors in the learned model get damped out rather than amplified.

Mathematically, contraction is defined by the largest eigenvalue of the Jacobian being less than 1. When this holds, feeding the output of one step as input to the next step shrinks distances exponentially. So even if step 50 makes a mistake and outputs an action that is 10 percent wrong, that mistake gets halved at step 51, quartered at step 52, and vanishes by step 100. The penalty during training enforces this exponential shrinkage.

In contrast, a non-contractive denoising model might have an eigenvalue of 1.01. Then a 0.1 percent error becomes 0.101 percent error at the next step, then 0.102 percent, and by step 100 that tiny mistake has become a 2 percent error, throwing off the final action. The contraction penalty prevents this.

stages.s: noisy action at step t (uncertain, has noise left)
learned denoising model removes one layer of noise
contraction penalty during training shrinks output sensitivity to input
denoising model outputs action at step t+1 (less noisy, close to step t if both inputs were close)
after 200 steps: clean action where small learned-model errors do not pile up into big mistakes

math.h2: The equation: score matching plus contraction penalty
math.words: loss equals diffusion-error loss plus gamma times contraction-loss, where diffusion-error measures how wrong the predicted noise removal is, and contraction-loss penalizes the largest eigenvalue of the score Jacobian if it exceeds 1
math.equation: L(theta) = E[(norm(epsilon_theta + sigma_t * grad log p_t(a_t|s))^2)] + gamma * max(0, lambda_max(J_epsilon_theta) - 1)^2
symbols: the learned denoising model's prediction of noise to remove
the known standard deviation of noise at step t
the true direction toward cleaner actions at step t
the Jacobian matrix: how the model's output changes per input change
the largest eigenvalue of that matrix
the tuning knob: how much to prioritize contraction over denoising accuracy

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose at step 50, the learned model predicts noise-to-remove = 2.5, but true noise = 2.3. Error loss = (2.5 - 2.3)^2 = 0.04.
Also suppose the Jacobian has largest eigenvalue lambda_max = 1.2 (the model is over-sensitive). Contraction penalty = (1.2 - 1.0)^2 = 0.04.
With gamma = 1, total loss for this step = 0.04 + 1 * 0.04 = 0.08.
The optimizer will reduce both: improve the noise prediction AND shrink the Jacobian (make the model less sensitive).
If lambda_max falls to 1.02, contraction penalty drops to (1.02 - 1)^2 = 0.0004, so most pressure shifts to improving denoising accuracy.

math.note: The contraction penalty forces the denoising model to be insensitive to input changes, so errors from imperfect learning do not compound across 200 steps.

charts.title: Naive diffusion policy (no contraction)
charts.note: Sensitive denoising path means errors compound; performance drops under data scarcity.

charts.title: Contractive Diffusion Policy (this paper)
charts.note: Funnel-like denoising path keeps error local; keeps performance high even when the learned model is imperfect or data is scarce.

items.html: If gamma is too large, the penalty dominates, and the model becomes so insensitive it forgets how to adjust to different states. The robot learns a one-action-fits-all policy.

items.b: Contraction does not fix bad data.
items.html: If the offline data contains only bad actions (e.g., a robot trained only on clumsy pickups), contraction will reliably produce a clumsy pick every time. Resistance to errors does not improve the quality of the underlying actions in the data, because contraction prevents errors from the learned model, not errors in the original data itself.
Computing the Jacobian and its largest eigenvalue at every training step adds overhead. For very large action spaces or long denoising chains, this can slow training.

Tune gamma carefully via validation data; use a recent contraction-aware diffusion solver at test time; validate on both high-data and low-data regimes. The contraction penalty is most valuable when data is scarce or the learned model is approximate.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple offline robot-learning task, like picking and placing a cube on a table using a short trajectory (20 steps). Collect only 50 past episodes of successful pickups, making the data scarce and noisy. Train both a standard diffusion policy and a contractive one on this scarce data. At test time, run 100 episodes with each policy and measure how often the robot successfully places the cube near the target location.
demo.metric_eq: success_rate = (number of successful placements) / (total episodes); standard_variance = variance of final placement positions; robustness = mean placement distance when adding 0.1-unit sensor noise to observations during inference
demo.closing: Contractive Diffusion Policy should have higher success rate and lower variance, especially when sensor noise is added, proving that contraction makes the denoising path stable under error.
